The converter keeps every letter, space, and line break, and it escapes quotes and backslashes so the JSON stays valid. A valid JSON file can be opened by any JSON reader, and the text inside it is exactly the text that went in.

The converter works through the list in order, reports each file as it finishes, and stops on a file it cannot read, saying which file failed and why, instead of skipping it silently. The list itself is never changed; only copies of the files are converted.

History

File formats grew up with computing itself. Plain text came first, words stored as plain letters with nothing else attached. Comma-separated values, CSV, spread through business in the 1970s as a plain way to move tables between machines. The JPEG picture format arrived in 1992, the PDF document format in 1993, and the PNG picture format in 1996. JSON, a plain way to write structured data, was set out by Douglas Crockford in 2001, and Markdown, a plain way to write formatted text, by John Gruber in 2004. Each new format solved one job well, and converters grew up to carry content between them, because no single format fits every job.
